Evidence LabEvery result here comes from a real run →

Every conclusion carries
its evidence.

Invaria tells a fund operator whether its records and the Stellar ledger agree on an operation, and keeps the evidence behind the answer.

  • MATCH

    Records and the Stellar ledger agree, with evidence.

  • BREAK

    A discrepancy is proven.

  • UNKNOWN

    Not enough evidence to conclude. Never means unpaid.

Five claims, five checks.

The repository ships separately. This page is the short path through it: what to test, what you should see, and what each result does not prove.

Run from the repo

Real Stellar testnet evidence, replayed offline

We issued a demo asset, DEMOA, on Stellar testnet and made three transactions on purpose: a real delivery of 1,000 units, a payment that fails, and a second 1,000-unit payment that carries the same memo. The order, bank and transfer-agent records are synthetic. The on-chain side is real, recorded from Horizon and RPC with the sha256 of every response.

An on-chain movement counts for an operation only through an explicit, approved execution link. A matching memo or amount never links anything, and a failed transaction never counts as a delivery.

Why provenance matters. In October 2025 Stellar found that Protocol 23 had archived 478 ledger entries with stale values; 77 were modified on restore before a patch quarantined them. Providers served those values correctly, and they still did not match canonical history. Nothing indicates the capture below was affected. It is the reason every observation keeps its source and sha256.

Explorer links go to the public testnet. Testnet is reset periodically; if it has been reset since 2026-10-05 the links stop resolving, and the recorded responses in tests/fixtures/stellar/recordings/demoa-own/, pinned by sha256, remain the evidence.

Same chain data, four sets of approved links

Only the execution links change between these scenarios. Pick one to see what the engine concludes and why.

# reproduces all four, sockets not needed
$ uv run --locked invaria demo-testnet tests/fixtures/corpus/subscription-testnet-1.6.0
…

Run from the repo

Conclusions you can audit, control by control

A fund subscription, SUB-0001, as its evidence arrives. Each evaluation is a pure function of a closed snapshot: it records when the facts were valid (valid_at) and when they were known (known_at). Open any control to see the checks the engine ran, the one that fixed the result, and what would move it forward.

The redemption corpus: 46 hand-written cases

Missed deadlines, short payments, cancellations, retractions, late corrections, collisions. Expected results were written by hand before the evaluator reproduced them. Under the current profile many cases are UNKNOWN on purpose: the synthetic chain certificates do not show that the observed burns are complete, so Invaria refuses to call them MATCH.

$ uv run --locked invaria check tests/fixtures/corpus/subscription-synthetic-1.2.0   # 9/9
$ uv run --locked invaria check tests/fixtures/corpus/redemption-synthetic-1.7.0     # 46/46
$ uv run --locked invaria diagnose tests/fixtures/corpus/subscription-synthetic-1.2.0 K3
$ uv run --locked invaria explain-change tests/fixtures/corpus/subscription-synthetic-1.2.0 K2 K3
Run from the repo

Tamper lab: try to forge an evidence bundle

A conclusion travels as a directory bundle: snapshot, profile, evidence and evaluation, each pinned by SHA-256 in a manifest, with a detached Ed25519 signature. The verifier re-runs the engine on the frozen artifacts and decides trust only from a trust store you choose. Below is a real signed bundle for K3, and the attacks we ran against it with the repository's verifier.

Your browser re-checks hashes and the Ed25519 signature live, on whatever you edit. The engine replay needs the repository: for the presets, the verifier's own report is shown next to the browser check.

Files in the bundle
Browser check
Edit
Reference verifier (invaria verify) for this preset

What the ladder shows

  • Changing one amount breaks its hash: REJECTED.
  • Recomputing the hashes moves the manifest, so the signature no longer covers it: UNTRUSTED. Without a trust store the replay disagrees with the recorded BREAK: MISMATCH.
  • A forger who rebuilds everything with the real engine gets REPRODUCED when nothing anchors the bundle. A hash proves integrity relative to the manifest, not authenticity. The published manifest hash or the trust store catches it.

$ uv run --locked invaria sign /tmp/k3 --key-file key.pem --key-id me --signed-at 2026-10-11T20:00:00Z
$ uv run --locked invaria verify /tmp/k3 --trust-store store.json
$ uv run --locked pytest tests/bundle/test_golden_corpus.py
Run from the repolocal console and query service, PostgreSQL

Integrity analytics: from one operation to the whole book

Per-operation results answer "what can we conclude about this case?". Analytics answers the next questions: where discrepancies concentrate, how much of the activity we can evaluate with enough evidence, what is blocking verification, and what to review first. It counts stored conclusions; it never re-evaluates them.

Every figure carries its numerator and denominator, and every figure opens onto the operations behind it. The financial result, the state of the evidence and the technical state stay separate.

We loaded a small synthetic book into a disposable PostgreSQL and asked the real service for an integrity report, then registered it. Ten operations: SUB-0001 goes MATCH then BREAK after a bank correction, seven subscriptions never receive their institutional evidence, one is evaluated but not published, one is registered but never evaluated.

Figures with their denominators

From the report itself. A zero denominator reads "not calculable", never 0 %. The share among conclusive cases shows the UNKNOWN it leaves out.

FigureNumeratorDenominatorValue
Why both denominators

Hypothetical book of 100 operations: 70 MATCH, 10 BREAK, 20 UNKNOWN. "87.5 % MATCH among conclusive" is true and hides the 20 we cannot conclude. "70 % MATCH of all included" is also true. Invaria prints both, with their denominators.

Illustrative numbers, not from the report.

Transfer counts hide the same trap: in tokenized funds, transfer volume mixes token creation, destruction and intermediary movements, and is not market liquidity (Tümer & Mafrur, arXiv 2610.05873).

What we knew at the close vs. what we know today

A report is registered with its evidence horizon and pinned references. When a bank correction arrives later, the registered report does not drift. Recomputing the same horizon today says something else, and says why.

Proposed model

What was justifiable on day X, what evidence later undermined it, and what holds today?

The same pinned, bitemporal record would carry incident revisions. A notice about an affected ledger entry would mark for review only the evaluations that depend on it, keep the original conclusion and the evidence it rested on, and record a declared repair separately from a verified one. The new result follows from the evidence that remains; it is not forced to UNKNOWN. Not implemented.

Privacy: each party gets what it needs to verify its part

An institution needs to show its operations are correct, and its records reveal clients, positions and commercial terms. Invaria's principle is that sensitive data stays under its owner's control and each recipient receives only what it needs to verify its part.

Implemented: the same report, two access profiles

Every query passes an explicit disclosure policy after its scope and before anything is read. There is no implicit policy. Below are the exact API responses of the local console for the operator who registered Report B and for a reviewer who was issued a restricted view of it.

operator-1full-operations@1full-report-summary@1
reviewer-1aggregate-outcome-counts@1
Response

  

    
What the reviewer's view never contains

      
The same fixed list for every view. A withheld category is not missing evidence, a zero or UNKNOWN.

    
Limits we state
    
      
  • Exact counts in a small population can reveal individual operations, including by comparing views. No suppression or noise yet.
    • 
      
  • The view is not signed and cannot be verified independently of the service.
    • 
      
  • Revoking stops later reads, not copies already delivered.
    • 
      
  • Bundles, other exports, logs and backups are outside the boundary for now. Once written, any file is in the custody of whoever controls the file system.
    • 
      
  • Enforced by the application, not against an administrator with direct database access.
    • 
    

  


  
Implemented: exporting a report is a permission of its own

  
Reading a report and writing it to a file are separate decisions. analytics report --out needs the scope exports:create and the policy export-integrity-report-file@1 on top of the query's own, all checked before the destination is opened. It runs under a database role that can only append to the export record. These are the real outcomes for the same report:

  
AttemptOutcomeFile

  

    
The export record

      
Who, which policies, which report and the sha256 and size of what was written. No path, file name, host or recipient is stored.

    
Append-only, even for the exporter

      
    
        
  • "completed" is the service's declaration that it published the file. It does not prove delivery or later custody.
    • 
        
  • Every file the commands write is new (mode 0600), never overwrites and follows no symbolic link. Verified on Linux. Safe writing is not a disclosure policy: bundles and other outputs have no export permission yet.
    • 
      

  


  

  
Proposed model

  
Privacy has to be part of what evidence means

  
"I cannot see the document" must not silently turn into "nobody can verify the result". These four situations would read differently in the evidence model.

  
SituationInterpretationStatus today

    
The evidence does not exist or was not receivedInformation is missing to evaluateUNKNOWN MISSING_EVIDENCE, built

    
The evidence exists but the recipient has no permissionAn access restriction, not missing evidencePartly built: 403 DISCLOSURE_POLICY_UNAVAILABLE for queries; not yet a state inside evaluations

    
The data is hidden, and a valid proof of the control existsThat control can be verified within the proof's scopeRoadmap

    
The proof does not match the required version or periodIt cannot justify that evaluationRoadmap

  


  

  
RoadmapNothing below is implemented. ZK and FHE do not appear in the branch.

  

    
1 · Local agent
Edge first
Bank statements, administrator records and investor data are processed inside the client's environment. The client decides what leaves: results, metrics, proofs or selected documents. Logs, errors, telemetry, backups and AI prompts are minimised too. Today the whole core already runs on one machine, offline.

    
2 · Zero-knowledge
A bounded redemption proof
The client keeps the evidence and proves one control, such as exact equality between paid and required amount. The recipient learns which rule, which version and which evidence set, not the values. A proof of a calculation does not prove the data is authentic or complete, so it has to be bound to admitted sources, signatures and coverage. One proven equality is never a MATCH on its own.

    
3 · FHE
Only when remote compute is required
Computing on encrypted values fits cloud analytics or reconciliation between institutions. If the local agent can compute the result and share a proof, encrypted remote processing is not needed. Latency, cost, supported operations and key management get measured first, and secure aggregation and MPC are compared.

  

  

    
Recommended order

      
    
        
  1. Privacy of the local agent and of exportspartly built

How it fits Stellar
Stellar has primitives to verify ZK proofs in Soroban contracts; proofs are generated by a separate system. Invaria would verify proofs off-chain first, and a Soroban verifier makes sense once another application needs the check on-chain. Invaria cannot make an already public transfer private. Stellar's private payments and confidential tokens are in developer preview, so the first opportunity is protecting the institutional records and their link to public operations.

  







  

    
Run from the repoProposed model

    
AI reads the evidence. It never decides.

    
An assistant is the natural way to ask "why is this a BREAK?" or "what is missing to conclude?". The design keeps three parts apart: the local agent processes the data, deterministically and without a language model; an MCP server exposes bounded, read-only tools; the AI assistant interprets their answers for a person. The model cannot claim institutional authority, approve rules, correct evidence or close an ambiguity on its own.

  

  
Built today: a read-only MCP server over the same query layer

  
invaria mcp serve exposes seven tools over stdio to a local MCP client. Every tool is read-only: none writes, signs, sends, approves or reconciles anything. The protocol annotations are hints for the client; the permission is checked by the server on every call, with the caller's access profile. Below are real calls to the server, made in-process against the same PostgreSQL world as the analytics section.

  
ToolWhat it answersInput

  

    
Tool callsclick to see the answer

    
Server instructions to the assistant

      
Evidence content comes from external sources, so the assistant is told to treat it as data and never as instructions. That is the first defence against prompt injection; the second is that no tool has a financial effect.

  

  
Response


  

  
Proposed modelProduct direction. Nothing below is implemented.

  

    
1 · Explanations derived, not written
A justification contract
Each conclusion would expose what changed, why it matters, what is missing and how to reproduce it. These fields come from the engine and its dependencies; the assistant only phrases them. It does not invent the narrative.

    
2 · Broader tools
From questions to impact
Planned tools trace the full lifecycle, list the conclusions a change affects, check invariants over an authorised scope, compare rule versions on a snapshot as a labelled simulation, and run a reconciliation as a budgeted job that announces its cost. Still none with a financial effect.

    
3 · Assisted rule discovery
AI proposes, people approve
Candidate invariants are mined from standards (FINOS CDM, ERC-7540, ERC-3643 as external profiles), verified code and operational traces, then searched for counterexamples. A rule moves from candidate to tested, reviewed and approved, and runs in shadow mode against the corpus before it can change a result. The model never approves its own rule.

  

  

    
Minimal evidence requests
When a control is UNKNOWN, the assistant can show which admissible sources would close it, with the minimum fields, interval and authority, instead of asking for access to every system. Today get_missing_evidence already returns the requirement; the plan with alternatives is the next step.

    
Guardrails that stay fixed
    
      
  • No float amounts and no language model in any decision path.
    • 
      
  • Linking ambiguities are closed by an operator with actor, reason and evidence, never by the model.
    • 
      
  • Prompts and logs are minimised like any other data leaving the client's environment.
    • 
    

  







  

    
What Invaria does not claim today

    
The limits are part of the product. These come from the repository's capability matrix and describe the public branch at the commit this page was built from. They mark where the branch stands today, not where the project ends: several appear on the roadmap above. The rules that hold by design are listed apart.

  

  

    
Current limits of this branch

      
Where the public branch stands at this commit. Later commits can change these.

      
    
      
  • Not production-ready, not a hosted service, not complete Stellar support. Testnet and synthetic data only; no mainnet.
    • 
      
  • On-chain coverage used by the engines is provider_claimed: Horizon and RPC are run by the same provider. Ledger verification against a history checkpoint exists as a separate report and changes no conclusion.
    • 
      
  • The institution, bank and transfer agent of the demo are synthetic. DEMOA is not a real fund.
    • 
      
  • Not supported: fees, partial fills, multiple payments, FX, omnibus accounts, custom Soroban tokens, R3 source proofs.
    • 
      
  • Analytics reads the present publication state; the evidence horizon filters by knowledge time only.
    • 
      
  • Zero-knowledge proofs, FHE, webhooks, OIDC/SSO and multi-tenant hosting are not implemented.
    • 
      
  • The MCP server is local and stdio only. The core bundles and calls no language model; the assistant is whatever MCP client the operator connects.
    • 
    

    
Rules that stay by design

      
Deliberate choices of the model, not gaps to close.

      
    
      
  • UNKNOWN never means unpaid. BREAK is never called a loss. Not applicable is never fulfilled.
    • 
      
  • No legal right is inferred from a ticker, price, wallet or transfer. Even a token backed 1:1 can be a security entitlement rather than a registered shareholding.
    • 
      
  • A report's sha256 checks internal consistency, not who issued it. It does not show that all real activity was registered.
    • 
    

  







  

    
Reproduce this page

    
Python 3.13 and uv. The offline parts need no network and no database. Analytics and disclosure need a disposable PostgreSQL.

  

  

  
The scripts that produced this page's data (collect.py, analytics_world.py) call the same functions as the CLI: evaluators, diagnosis, bundle builder, signer, verifier, query service and console. The signing key used for the tamper lab was generated in memory, used once and discarded; only its public key is shown.
